spec.text: Right to privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty and is inherently protected under Article 21 of the constitution. Explain. In this reference discuss the law relating to D.N.A. testing of child in the womb to establish its paternity.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-four. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Explain why privacy sits under Article twenty-one. Then discuss the law on a DNA test of a child in the womb, to prove paternity. Here is the strange part. We found no Supreme Court ruling on that second half.

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Explain, then discuss. That is three jobs. Show why privacy sits in Article twenty-one. Give the law on paternity tests. Then deal with the child, and the womb.

spec.title: Privacy, Article 21 and the DNA Paternity Test

lines.text: The word privacy is nowhere in the Constitution.
In twenty seventeen, nine judges found it inside Article twenty-one.
It is the core of human dignity.

scenes.vo: Start with the right. The word privacy is nowhere in the Constitution. In twenty seventeen, nine judges found it inside Article twenty-one. It is the core of human dignity.

lines.text: But the right is not absolute.
A law must pass three tests.
Legality, a legitimate aim, and proportionality.
A court's order for a DNA test must pass the same kind of weighing.

lines.text: Section one-twelve of the Evidence Act says a child born in marriage is conclusively legitimate.
Only proof of no access breaks it.
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam repeats it, in section one-sixteen.

scenes.vo: Now paternity. Section one-twelve of the Evidence Act says a child born in marriage is conclusively legitimate. Only proof of no access breaks it. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam repeats it, in section one-sixteen.

spec.title: Privacy, Article 21 and the DNA Paternity Test

lines.text: In Goutam Kundu, no test as a matter of course.
In Bhabani Prasad Jena, only on eminent need.
In Dipanwita Roy, a test was allowed on a specific plea.
And Firodia, in twenty twenty-three, refused it for a child.

scenes.vo: So courts are careful. In Goutam Kundu, no test as a matter of course. In Bhabani Prasad Jena, only on eminent need. In Dipanwita Roy, a test was allowed on a specific plea. And Firodia, in twenty twenty-three, refused it for a child.

spec.title: Privacy, Article 21 and the DNA Paternity Test

lines.text: But all these cases concern a child already born.
For the womb, the nearest law is the PC-PNDT Act.
Section four allows pre-natal tests only for listed conditions.

scenes.vo: But all these cases concern a child already born. For the womb, the nearest law is the PC-PNDT Act. Section four allows pre-natal tests only for listed conditions. Paternity is not among them.

blocks.text: _Puttaswamy_ (2017) held privacy an intrinsic part of life and liberty under Article 21; a paternity test tests that right against a court's search for truth.
1. Privacy within Article 21

• Nine judges (2017): privacy is protected under Article 21 and Part III, though the word is not in the Constitution. • _Dignity_: 'the constitutional core of human dignity'; it covers family life and procreation. • Not absolute: _legality, need, proportionality_.
2. DNA test to prove paternity

• Section 112, Evidence Act (now s.116, BSA 2023): birth in marriage is _conclusive proof_ of legitimacy unless non-access. • Courts allow a test only on 'eminent need' and a strong prima facie case (_Bhabani Prasad Jena_, _Goutam Kundu_); never exploratory. • _Sharda v Dharmpal_: a test is not per se against Article 21, but not mechanical. • _Dipanwita Roy_: allowed on a specific non-access plea; refusal may draw an adverse inference, which is discretionary.
A flow: presumption, then a strong prima facie case, then eminent need weighed against the child's privacy, then an order, or a refusal.
blocks.label: Fig. 1: When a court orders a paternity test

blocks.text: 3. The child and the womb

• _Firodia_ (2023) refused a test of the child: legitimacy is 'an essential attribute of the right to privacy'; 'the child cannot be used as a pawn'. • PC-PNDT Act, s.4(2): pre-natal tests only for listed conditions; paternity is not one. • We found no Supreme Court ruling on a foetal paternity test; these rules apply by analogy.
So privacy shields the child from casual tests; a court orders one only on eminent need, and the womb limb has no ruling we could find.

scenes.vo: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open with Puttaswamy and the clash it sets up. That one line frames the whole answer.

scenes.vo: Section three is the child. Use Firodia: legitimacy is part of a child's privacy. The child cannot be used as a pawn. Then state the limit honestly. We found no Supreme Court ruling on a foetal paternity test.

weak.text: A husband can get a DNA test of the child whenever he doubts paternity.
weak.miss: courts refuse a test on a mere asking; eminent need and a prima facie case are needed

weak.text: The section 112 presumption falls once a DNA test is sought.
weak.miss: birth in marriage is conclusive proof unless non-access is shown

weak.text: Pre-natal DNA tests are allowed to settle paternity.
weak.miss: PC-PNDT s.4(2) lists the permitted purposes; paternity is not one

weak.text: Privacy is an absolute right under Article 21.
weak.miss: it must pass legality, need and proportionality
the word 'privacy' appears nowhere in the Constitution

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It says a husband can get a test whenever he doubts. Courts refuse that. It says pre-natal tests can settle paternity. The PC-PNDT Act does not allow that. It says privacy is absolute. It is not. And it says privacy is written in Article twenty-one. The word is not there.
